Commentators point out that the question is not really a question. The passage says so directly: they raised him only for the sake of a dispute, and calls them a people fond of quarrelling. The complaint is about method, not about the doctrine underneath.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The context was an argument about what happens to objects of worship and to those worshipped without their consent, and the objectors saw an opening they could exploit. Commentators differ on the details of the exchange and record more than one account of what was said. What the ayat report clearly is the tactic: a comparison offered in order to win an argument rather than to reach anything.

keyTerms.note: A word for people who went ahead, used of predecessors whose case is settled. It occurs only here in this form, and it makes a destroyed people into a reference for later ones.
The word carries two readings in the recitation tradition, one meaning to raise a din and the other to turn aside, and the commentators record both without deciding between them.
An intensive form occurring only here, from the root for adversaries in a dispute. It names a disposition rather than a position, describing people who argue as a habit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debate was a spectator sport in Mecca. Men gathered at the assembly and at the seasonal fairs to watch arguments the way they watched poetry contests, and a clever move was appreciated on its own terms whether or not it settled anything. A point that silenced an opponent was worth having regardless of whether it was true. The passage names that culture and declines to play in it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the audience's reaction here is read two different ways in the recitation tradition, one giving a sense of clamour and the other of turning aside, and both readings are transmitted. The word for their quarrelsomeness at the end of the passage occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and neither does the word used for the drowned as a precedent.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes between raising a question and using one. What is criticised is not the difficulty of the comparison but the purpose behind it, which is to win rather than to find out. That distinction is worth holding because the same words can be said in both spirits. It also declines to be drawn: the surah simply names what is happening and moves to the answer in the next ayah, without contesting the point.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answer immediately, describing him as a servant favoured and made an example for a people.
Addresses the underlying question about what is worshipped, and exempts those already destined for good.
Says the human being is the most contentious of things, naming the disposition this passage identifies.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you make a point in an argument that you would not defend if you were alone. It happens quickly and it feels like winning. This passage does not say the point was wrong; it says why it was raised. That is a question you can only ask about yourself.

studies.title: A Sign That The Hour Is Coming
studies.meaning: The answer is deliberately plain. He was only a servant on whom favour was placed, made an example for the Children of Israel. Then a reminder that God could have made successors on earth out of angels instead, which removes any argument from what a creature happens to be. The last line has been read in more than one way: some take the pronoun as the son of Mary, whose return is a sign of the Hour, others as the recitation, which gives knowledge of it. A transmitted variant reads the word as a marker. The instruction after it is the same either way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, answering an argument the objectors had raised in the previous ayat. Commentators note that the surah replies with a description rather than a rebuttal, since the position it is correcting was never actually held by those who made the point. The mention of the Children of Israel places the example in its own setting. No specific occasion is reported for these three ayat.

keyTerms.note: The Quran's highest ordinary description of a human being, used of prophets at their most honoured moments. Placed first in the sentence, it settles the category before anything else is said.
A verb for taking someone's place in turn, occurring only here in this form. It describes generations following each other, which is what the hypothetical would replace with angels.
The word appears in this exact form only here. A transmitted variant reading gives instead a word for a marker or landmark, and both are preserved in the recitation tradition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Landmarks were how Arabia navigated. A known rock, a solitary tree, a ridge with a name told a traveller where he was and how far remained, and guides described routes by listing them in order. A marker did not cause the destination or explain it; it told you the journey was under way and roughly how much was left. That is the register the ayah's closing image belongs to.
studies.didYouKnow: The word in the last line of this passage occurs in this exact form only here in the Quran, and the recitation tradition preserves a second reading of it, differing by one vowel and giving the sense of a landmark rather than of knowledge. Both readings are transmitted and both are recited, and the instruction that follows the phrase is identical either way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage settles a dispute by naming a category rather than by arguing. Servanthood is not a demotion in the Quran's vocabulary; it is the description applied to those closest to God. The hypothetical about angels then removes the assumption behind the whole quarrel, that being a certain kind of creature confers standing. What remains at the end is not a claim to be assessed but an instruction: follow, and the path is straight.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same self-description from the child in the cradle, calling himself a servant of God given the Book.
States that he would never disdain to be a servant of God, and neither would the angels brought near.
Answers the same assumption, saying that if angels walked the earth an angel messenger would have been sent.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are waiting for and ask what the last clear marker was that told you the journey is still moving. Not the destination, a marker. Write it down. This passage ends with a sign rather than a date, and living with signs rather than dates is a skill that has to be practised.

studies.title: To Make Some Of It Clear
studies.meaning: A warning first: do not let the adversary turn you aside, since he is an open enemy. The verb is the same one used a few lines earlier for the audience's reaction to a comparison, which quietly links the two. Then Jesus arrives with clear proofs and states his errand in his own words. I have come to you with wisdom, and to make clear to you part of what you differ about. Commentators dwell on that word part. The mission is described as limited from inside it, by the one carrying it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a section responding to an argument raised about the son of Mary. The Quran gives him direct speech here rather than describing him, which is how it usually answers claims made about a prophet. Commentators note the community he addressed was already divided over questions of law and practice. No specific occasion is reported for these two ayat.

keyTerms.gloss: let him not turn you aside
keyTerms.note: An emphatic form of the verb for diverting someone from a route. The same root described the audience's reaction a few ayat earlier, so the surah uses one word for both movements.
From a root that also gives the words for judgement and for a bridle. Wisdom in this vocabulary is what restrains and steers, rather than an accumulation of things known.
A plain partitive. Its presence limits the claim being made: the errand is to clarify some of what they disagree about, not all of it, and the limit is stated by the speaker himself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration in Arabia was usually partial by design. A judge was asked to settle a specific dispute, not to reorganise everything between two clans, and both sides knew in advance what was in front of him and what was not. A man who tried to settle more than he had been asked to settle would have lost the confidence of both parties. Limited errands were the normal shape of authority.
studies.didYouKnow: This root for turning aside appears at three separate points in the surah: hindering people from the path, the audience's reaction when a comparison was raised, and the adversary's diverting warned against here. Two of the three occur within six ayat of each other, so one word carries most of the movement away from the subject in this section.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a limit inside a prophetic mission and has the prophet state it. Not everything a community argues about was on the agenda, which is a striking thing for a revelation to record. It also joins wisdom to clarification rather than to knowledge as such. What is offered is not more information but the sorting of some of what was already in dispute, which is a different and harder service.

crossReferences.why: Lists what was given to him, including the Book and wisdom, in a passage recounting the same mission.
Gives a longer version of the same address, including making lawful part of what had been forbidden.
Describes wisdom as given to whom God wills, and calls it much good for whoever receives it.

studies.applyIt: Pick one disagreement you keep trying to settle entirely and decide which single part of it you could actually clarify this month. Then do only that part. This ayah has a prophet naming the limits of his own errand, which makes the instinct to fix everything look less like diligence than it usually feels.

studies.title: My Lord And Your Lord
studies.meaning: The speech ends in a sentence with no room in it. God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path. Commentators note that the same phrase is placed in the mouths of several prophets across the Quran, always at the point where a mission is summarised. Then the report of what happened next: the factions differed among themselves, and woe is pronounced on the wrongdoers. The last line turns to the present audience with a question about what exactly they are waiting for, given that the Hour arrives suddenly and unnoticed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The mention of factions differing refers to divisions that arose among communities given earlier revelation, which the Quran treats throughout as a warning to the community now forming. Commentators read the sequence as a single argument: the message was plain, the division came afterwards, and delay is not neutral. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A plural for organised groups formed around a position. Using it for people who divided over a prophet describes them as having become parties rather than as having reached different conclusions.
An exclamation of doom rather than a description. Arabic uses it for a cry raised over someone, so the sentence changes register from report to something closer to a lament.
A word for something arriving with no approach that could be watched. The Quran uses it repeatedly of the Hour, always paired with people being occupied with something else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian life was built around things you could see coming. Caravans were expected within a range of days, seasons announced themselves, and a raid was preceded by rumours carried between camps. Genuine suddenness was rare and therefore frightening: a flash flood down a dry valley, a well found empty. That specific kind of arrival, with no signs to read beforehand, is what this word names.
studies.didYouKnow: The declaration that God is my Lord and your Lord is given in the Quran to more than one prophet, appearing in nearly identical words in several surahs and always at the summarising moment of a mission. Here it is followed immediately by the report that the factions divided, so the Quran places the plainest possible statement directly beside the division that came after it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the beginning of division after the message rather than in it, which is a recurring claim across this surah. It also treats waiting as a position rather than a suspension of judgement. The question in the last line assumes that everyone is doing something while the Hour approaches, and that not deciding is one of the things a person can be doing when it arrives without warning.

crossReferences.why: Gives the identical declaration in another surah, followed by the same statement that the factions differed.
Repeats the same words in a longer account of the same mission, calling it a straight path.
Describes the Hour as arriving only suddenly, and says it weighs heavily on the heavens and the earth.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you are waiting for before making one particular change you already believe in. Name the condition out loud: more time, more certainty, a better week. Then ask whether the condition is something you would recognise if it arrived. This ayah is a question about waiting, and most waiting turns out to have no stated end.

studies.title: Friends Will Be Enemies
studies.meaning: The opening line is a statement about friendship, not about enemies. On that day close friends turn on one another, and one group is excepted. Early scholars read it as a claim about what the friendships were built on. Those that held people to something survive. Those that helped people avoid it become accusations. Then the address shifts into the second person, and fear and grief are both lifted. The entry described is not solitary. Spouses go in together, and that is stated as part of the welcome.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been describing a society defending inherited practice on the ground that the fathers did it. It also describes companions who confirm one another in exactly that. This passage arrives after a statement in the voice of Jesus about worship and a straight path. It also follows a note that the parties differed among themselves. Friendship as a way of drifting is one of this surah's running concerns.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to penetrate or run all the way through something. Such a friend has entered a person's character rather than standing beside it, which is why the reversal described is so total.
The same word the Quran uses for matched pairs generally. Placing it inside the invitation makes the entry a shared arrival rather than an individual verdict delivered separately.
From a root joining beauty to gladness, related to the word for fine ornamented cloth. It describes joy that shows outwardly, the delight of someone being received well.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Friendship in Arabia was formal and public. Men were paired as companions for journeys and campaigns. A person's name was shaped more by whose company they kept than by their own conduct. Onlookers had nothing else to go on. Choosing companions was understood as choosing a direction, and families stepped in on the choice. The word used here names the closest form of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for these friends comes from a root meaning to run all the way through something. Such a friend has got inside a person, rather than standing beside them. The same root gives the title the Quran uses of Abraham. He is called the close friend of God. So one word covers the highest and the most dangerous form of the same closeness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Friendship is treated as a moral tool, not as a private pleasure. The passage does not say that friendships end. It says they flip. That implies they were doing something all along that will one day become visible. And the reversal is stated with an exception, so the cure offered is not being alone. What changes the outcome is the character of the friendship, not whether you have one.

crossReferences.why: Gives the regret from inside: a man who took someone as a friend and was turned from the reminder.
Uses the same word for Abraham, showing the closeness this ayah warns about at its best.
Describes the companion assigned to one who turns away, and the wish for distance on that day.

studies.applyIt: Think about which of your friendships produces the version of you that you would want recorded, and which produces the one you would not. You already know both answers. Put an hour in the calendar this month for the first person, by name, at a time. That is the whole exercise, and it is harder than it sounds.
studies.explainEasier: On that day, close friends will turn against each other. Only good people are left out of this. God tells the ones who believed and obeyed not to be afraid or sad. They are told to enter the Garden with their partners, happy.

studies.title: Whatever Delights The Eyes
studies.meaning: Service is described before contents. Trays of gold and cups are carried round to them, and only then does the sentence name what is in the Garden: whatever the souls desire and the eyes take pleasure in. Commentators note the two faculties are given separately, appetite and sight, so the promise covers what a person wants and what they simply enjoy looking at. Then a clause that changes everything the description would otherwise mean: and you will remain in it. The word for lasting is what the gold of this surah has been denied throughout.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the passage describing what waits for those who believed and submitted, immediately after they are told they will not fear or grieve. Commentators note the pointed use of gold here, in a surah named for gold ornament and largely spent dismissing it. The audience included believers with nothing, hearing a description built out of the very objects their opponents were being told meant nothing.

keyTerms.note: A passive from the verb for circling, the same root as the circuit made around the sanctuary. The servers are left unnamed, so the sentence describes attention without describing anyone giving it.
A plural for broad shallow platters used for serving food to a group. It occurs only here, and it belongs to hospitality on a large scale rather than to individual portions.
A verb for taking pleasure in something. Attaching it to the eyes rather than to the person makes enjoyment through looking a category of its own, separate from the desiring named just before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality in Arabia was performed rather than merely provided. Food came round on a common platter that guests ate from together, and the number of dishes and the quality of the vessels announced a host's standing before anyone tasted anything. Gold vessels were beyond the reach of almost everyone. Describing the Garden this way used the grammar of welcome that every listener could read.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is named for gold ornament and spends most of its length treating such things as worthless, then describes the Garden with trays of gold. The word for the wide serving platters occurs only in this ayah. What separates the two treatments is not the material but the clause at the end of this line, which says the state described will not end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not spiritualise the reward. It keeps the objects and changes their duration, which is a more interesting move than replacing them would be. Everything the surah has dismissed was dismissed as the goods of a life that stops, and here the same goods appear with that limit removed. The promise also covers pleasure that has no use, since delighting the eyes serves nothing beyond itself.

crossReferences.why: Promises whatever the souls desire in nearly the same words, spoken there by angels rather than described.
Describes vessels and cups carried round in the same way, made of silver and measured exactly.
Gives this surah's verdict on the same objects when they belong to the present life, calling them its goods.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing today that you enjoy purely by looking at it and that serves no purpose: a colour, a bird, someone's handwriting. Do not photograph it. This ayah names delight of the eyes as its own category, separate from wanting, and most of us have stopped counting that as anything at all.

studies.title: A Garden You Were Made To Inherit
studies.meaning: The Garden is described with a verb of inheritance rather than of purchase, and yet the clause that follows attaches it to what they used to do. Commentators hold both together: the deeds are the reason and the estate is still a gift, since nothing anyone does buys such a thing. Fruit is named as the one contents. Then the passage turns and gives the other outcome in two lines, with the second doing the real work. It will not be lightened for them, and they are inside it in despair, the word for a person whose expectation has run out.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's paired descriptions of the two outcomes before it returns to argument. Commentators note the brevity on both sides compared with other surahs; the Garden gets two lines and the Fire two. The audience were people who had lost property and standing in the city, which gives the vocabulary of inheritance a particular weight here. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.gloss: you were made to inherit it
keyTerms.note: A passive from the vocabulary of estates. An inheritance is received rather than earned, yet it goes to particular people for particular reasons, which is why the next clause fits beside it.
An intensive passive from the root for easing off and growing weak. What is denied is not release but the ordinary tendency of anything intense to lose force over time.
From a root for being cut off from hope and falling silent because there is nothing left to say. The word occurs four times in the Quran, each time of people at the moment a matter closes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance was the main way property moved in Arabia, and everyone knew the difference between what a man had built and what had come to him. An inherited estate was still his, and nobody thought less of him for it, but nobody credited him with making it either. That double sense, fully yours and not of your making, is exactly what this ayah's verb carries.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for despair at the end of this passage occurs in four places in the Quran, and a related verb in a fifth. Every one describes people at the moment a matter closes: seized suddenly while enjoying what they were given, standing when the Hour arrives, or waiting for a mercy that does not come. The root means falling silent because nothing more can be said.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage keeps reward and inheritance in the same sentence without resolving the tension, and the tension is the point. Deeds matter and do not purchase; the Garden is deserved and is still received. On the other side, what is described is not the intensity of the Fire but its refusal to fade, which addresses the one hope a person in pain actually holds on to, that things ease with time.

crossReferences.why: Names the inheritors who will inherit the highest gardens, using the same vocabulary of estate for the reward.
Has those entering say they were guided to it, and that they were made to inherit it for what they did.
Describes a place where no fatigue or weariness touches them, the reverse of what is denied here.

studies.applyIt: Think of one good thing in your life that you both worked for and were handed. Name the part you did and the part you did not. Most people can do this in a minute and find the second list longer. This ayah puts earning and inheriting in one sentence, and it does not try to separate them either.

studies.title: You Are Staying Here
studies.meaning: A denial comes first, before anyone has objected: We did them no wrong, but they were the wrongdoers. Then the only exchange of dialogue in the scene. They call to the keeper of the Fire asking that his Lord finish them off, and the reply is three words long. You are staying. Commentators note that the request is for extinction rather than release, and that the answer neither refuses nor explains. The passage then states what most people actually dislike, which is the truth itself, and asks whether they have settled some scheme.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's closing sequence of warnings. Commentators note that the keeper of the Fire is named here and nowhere else in the Quran, a detail preserved without any further account of him. The reference to a scheme being fixed connects to plots against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that the Meccan surahs mention repeatedly. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for bringing something to a definite end. What is requested is not relief or release but termination, which is a different and darker thing to be asking for.
A participle for lingering in a place, an unremarkable everyday word. Its plainness against the extremity of the request is what gives the reply its weight in Arabic.
A verb for twisting strands into a firm cord, hence settling a matter definitively. Both this verb and its answering participle occur only in this ayah, and only here in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rope-making supplied Arabic with its vocabulary for settling things. To twist strands into a cord was to make a matter firm, and to untwist one was to break an agreement. Both images appear in this surah within thirty ayat of each other. An audience that made cordage by hand heard the metaphor as a description of work rather than as a figure of speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The keeper of the Fire is named in this ayah and in no other place in the Quran, and his entire recorded speech is three words in Arabic. Both the verb for twisting a scheme tight and the participle answering it occur only in this passage, so a short exchange contains three words the text never uses again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage opens by denying injustice before any complaint has been made, which places the question of fairness at the front rather than leaving it implied. It then makes its strongest claim in passing: most people dislike the truth. That is offered as an explanation of the whole surah's reception, and it locates the difficulty not in the evidence or the argument but in what people would prefer to be the case.

crossReferences.why: States the same denial, that God did not wrong them but they were wronging themselves all along.
Gives a similar plea from inside, asking to be taken out, and receives an equally short reply.
Describes those plotting against the Prophet, and says God plans while they plan, as this passage does.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what true thing you would least like to be true about your own life. Not about the world, about you. Sit with it for two minutes without deciding whether it is. This passage says plainly that most people dislike the truth, and the only place you can test that claim is on yourself.

studies.title: Their Whispering Is Written Down
studies.meaning: A question about what they assume: do they reckon We do not hear their secret and their private conference. The answer is a single particle of correction, and then a detail that goes further than the denial. Our messengers are with them, writing. Commentators identify these as recording angels, and note the shift from hearing to writing, which is a stronger claim. Then a statement offered in the plainest terms available: if the Merciful had a child, I would be the first to worship. The surah closes the passage by declaring the Lord of the Throne beyond what they describe.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Private consultation among the leading families about how to handle the Prophet was a real and frequent activity, and the Quran refers to it in several places. Commentators read the offer in the second ayah as a way of showing that the objection is not being resisted out of stubbornness. No specific occasion is reported. The final glorification is a formula the Quran uses to close arguments about God's nature.

keyTerms.note: A word for people drawing aside to speak where others cannot hear. It names the meeting rather than what is said in it, so a gathering itself is what is being described as known.
A particle used only to contradict a negative. It cannot answer an ordinary question, so its presence marks the previous sentence as an assumption being overturned rather than a query answered.
The verb for setting out a description of something. Placing God beyond what they describe rules out the whole activity, not just the particular descriptions being offered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's decisions were made in private consultation and announced afterwards. Men withdrew to a house or a corner of the assembly, agreed a line, and presented it as a settled position. Everyone knew this happened and nobody knew the contents, which was the point. The word this ayah uses names that specific social form, the drawing aside, rather than any particular conversation.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for private conference used here occurs in this exact form twice in the Quran, once about the leading men of Mecca and once in a passage about those who concealed their intentions in Medina. Both times it is paired with the word for what is kept secret, so the Quran names the private thought and the private meeting together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage moves from being heard to being written, which changes what is at stake. A remark overheard can be denied; a record cannot. Then the hypothetical offer makes an important point about the shape of the disagreement. What is being refused is not a claim someone would rather not accept, but one that is not true, and the speaker says he would be first in line if it were.

crossReferences.why: Says no three confer privately without God being with them, whatever the number of those meeting.
Describes God nearer than the jugular vein, with two receivers seated and recording every utterance.
Uses the identical closing formula, declaring the Lord of Might beyond what they attribute to Him.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have said in a private group chat this month that you would not say in the main one. You do not need to delete it. Just notice that you keep two registers, and ask which of them you would call your actual view. This ayah is about the gap between the two.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Leave Them To Their Game
studies.meaning: An instruction that sounds like surrender and is not. Leave them to plunge in and to play until they meet the Day they are promised. Commentators note the two verbs: one for wading into deep talk without footing, one for occupying oneself with what has no outcome. The sentence sets both against a deadline, which is what makes the leaving possible. Then the surah states its position in a single line built on repetition. He is the one who is God in the heaven and God in the earth, and He is the Wise, the Knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the surah's close, after a long sequence of quoted objections and answers. Commentators read the instruction as marking the end of an argument rather than the abandonment of an audience, since the surah continues to address them for several more lines. The setting is a city where the Prophet had been arguing publicly for years with visibly diminishing returns.

keyTerms.note: A verb for stepping into water deeper than you can stand in. The Quran uses it for talk that goes past what the speaker knows, so the image is of losing the bottom without noticing.
The ordinary verb for a child's play. Placed beside the previous word, it describes activity that is absorbing and produces nothing, which is the whole assessment being made.
The word is repeated in the same line, once for the heaven and once for the earth. Arabic could have said it once; the repetition is what makes the sentence answer a division people actually made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian religion was regional. A god had a place, a shrine and a territory, and people appealed to whichever one governed where they were or what they were doing. Travellers made offerings on entering new ground. A statement that the same one is God in the sky and God on the ground cut against the working assumption of everyone who had ever changed patrons when they changed locations.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a god is repeated twice within this single short line, once for the heaven and once for the earth, in a construction the Quran uses nowhere else in quite this form. The sentence spends its length insisting on sameness across two places, which is not how a claim about a single God usually needs to be phrased.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models an ending to argument that is neither agreement nor contempt. The instruction is to leave, and what makes leaving bearable is the deadline named in the same sentence. Then the following line states the position without addressing anyone, which is what a settled conviction sounds like when it stops being defended. The two moves belong together: you can only stop arguing if you still know what you hold.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to leave them plunging in their play, after telling the Prophet to say one word.
Repeats the instruction almost exactly, telling him to leave them until they meet their promised Day.
States the same universal ownership at greater length, with the heavens and the earth both belonging to Him.

studies.applyIt: Pick one argument you have been having on and off for years with somebody who will not move. Decide today to stop having it, and write down in one sentence what you actually believe so that stopping is not the same as giving it up. This ayah pairs leaving with a statement, and the statement is the part that makes leaving possible.

studies.title: Blessed Is The One Who Owns
studies.meaning: Three things are joined in a single sentence and the joining is the argument. Sovereignty over the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, knowledge of the Hour held with Him, and the returning of everyone to Him. Commentators note that the middle clause answers a question the surah has raised twice already, and answers it by relocating rather than informing. The opening word is a verb of blessedness used in the Quran only of God, and it describes overflowing abundance rather than a blessing conferred by anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's final movement. Questions about when the Hour would arrive were among the standing Meccan challenges, and the Quran answers them consistently by naming who holds the knowledge instead of supplying a date. Commentators report no occasion for the ayah. Its placement immediately after a statement that God is God in the heaven and in the earth continues the same widening of scope.

keyTerms.note: From a root for something that settles, remains and increases, used of a kneeling camel and of water pooling. It is applied in the Quran only to God, and it names abundance that stays.
A formula the Quran uses to close a description of the heavens and earth. It rules out any gap or intermediate region that might fall outside what has just been claimed.
The phrase places the knowledge with Him rather than describing the Hour itself. What is being answered is not when it comes but who is in a position to say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ownership in Arabia was demonstrated by knowing. A man who owned a herd could tell you where each animal was, what it had cost and what it would fetch, and a claim to property that came without that knowledge was not taken seriously. Joining sovereignty and knowledge in one sentence used a test the audience applied every day in the market.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb opening this ayah is used in the Quran only with God as its subject, and never in a form that would let a human being be its object. Its root is the one behind the word for a camel kneeling to rest and for a pool where water gathers and stays, so the blessing it names is settledness and increase rather than something bestowed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ties three claims together so that none stands alone. Ownership without knowledge would be mere possession; knowledge without return would leave the matter unresolved; return without ownership would raise the question of who is receiving anyone. Put in one sentence, they describe a situation with no loose ends, which is what makes the unanswered question about timing sit differently than it otherwise would.

crossReferences.why: Lists knowledge of the Hour first among the things kept with God alone, alongside rain and what wombs carry.
Opens a surah with the same verb of blessedness, applied to the one who sent down the criterion.
Answers the direct question about the Hour by saying its knowledge is with the Lord alone.

studies.applyIt: Take one question about the future that you have looked up more than three times this month: a forecast, a result, a date. Notice that repeating the search has produced no new knowledge. This ayah does not tell you to stop caring. It tells you where the answer is kept, which is at least a reason to stop refreshing.

studies.title: Turn Aside And Say Peace
studies.meaning: Intercession is closed off and then reopened by a narrow clause: those called on besides Him hold no power to intercede, except whoever bore witness to the truth and does so knowingly. Then the surah's last three lines move quickly. Ask them who created them and they will say God, so how are they turned away. The Prophet's own words are quoted, that these are a people who do not believe. And the answer given to him is not an argument but an instruction: turn aside from them and say peace. They will come to know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that has spent most of its length in argument. Commentators note that the closing instruction belongs to the period before any change in the community's position, when nothing could be done about the opposition and something still had to be said to them. The complaint quoted in the second-to-last ayah is the only place in the surah where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) speaks in his own voice.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make a pair, adding oneself alongside a petitioner. The exception clause ties the ability entirely to having borne witness to the truth with knowledge.
A noun for an utterance, occurring only here in the Quran. Using a noun rather than a verb turns the Prophet's complaint into a thing that was said, quoted and set down.
From the root for the side or face, meaning to turn away and, by extension, to overlook. The same root opened the surah, where withdrawing the Reminder was raised and rejected.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Greeting decided everything in Arabia. Whether you gave a man peace on the road, and whether he returned it, announced the state of things between your families to anyone watching. Withholding it was a declaration. Being told to turn aside and still give the greeting was being told to hold two positions at once, which everyone present would have understood as a difficult thing to carry off.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that closes this surah, telling the Prophet to turn aside, comes from the same root as the word in the surah's fifth ayah, where turning the Reminder away from a people who go too far was raised as a possibility and declined. The surah opens with God not turning away and ends with the Prophet being told to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ends an argument with a greeting rather than a verdict, which is a striking place to leave a surah of this length. The instruction is neither agreement nor hostility, and the final clause supplies the reason it can be held: they will come to know, which means the outcome is not being conceded, only postponed. Peace here is what conviction sounds like when it stops needing to win now.

crossReferences.why: Describes servants of the Merciful answering the ignorant with peace, the same response given as a habit.
Gives the same instruction to turn aside with a fair turning away, tied to the certainty of the coming Hour.
Has believers respond to idle talk by declaring peace on the speakers and stating their own position.

studies.applyIt: Choose one person you have quietly stopped greeting properly because of a disagreement. Greet them warmly this week without raising the matter. You are not conceding anything. This surah ends an argument it has been running for eighty ayat with a greeting, and it does not withdraw a single thing it said.
